value.overview: The Tropical Mockingbird (Mimus gilvus) is a medium-sized songbird of open and partly developed landscapes in the tropical Americas. It is known for its varied, repeated song and its ability to live near people. The species often forages on the ground or in low vegetation, feeding on insects, fruit, and other small food items. In Costa Rica, it is a locally distributed resident associated mainly with warm lowland habitats, especially in the northwest and along parts of the Pacific side.
value.classification: The Tropical Mockingbird belongs to the mockingbird family Mimidae and the genus Mimus. It is one of several closely related mockingbirds found in the Americas.
value.identification: This mockingbird is about 23–26 cm long and has a slim body, long tail, and fairly long bill. Its plumage is mostly gray above and paler below, with darker wings and tail that may show whitish edges or patches in flight. The face is plain compared with some other mockingbirds. It frequently raises or flicks its tail while walking or feeding. Its loud, varied song may include imitations and repeated phrases.
value.rangeHabitat: The Tropical Mockingbird ranges from Mexico through Central America and much of northern and central South America. In Costa Rica, it occurs as a resident rather than only as a seasonal migrant, but its distribution is uneven. It is most reliably associated with warm lowlands and dry or seasonally dry areas, including open woodland, scrub, pasture edges, agricultural land, gardens, villages, and other human-modified habitats. It is especially characteristic of suitable lowland sites in Guanacaste and other parts of the Pacific region.
value.migrationStatus: Generally resident in Costa Rica and across most of its range. Individuals may make local movements in response to food, breeding conditions, or habitat changes, but the species is not considered a regular long-distance migrant.
value.breeding: The Tropical Mockingbird usually breeds in shrubs, small trees, and other vegetation that provides cover. The nest is a bulky cup made from twigs, grass, and plant fibers, and is commonly placed above the ground. Both adults may defend a territory and help care for the young. Breeding timing varies across the broad range and is influenced by local rainfall and habitat conditions. In Costa Rica, nesting may occur during favorable periods in the dry or wet season depending on region.
value.dietFeeding: Its diet includes insects and other small invertebrates, berries, and a variety of fruits. It commonly searches on the ground, moving through short grass, leaf litter, paths, lawns, and open soil. It also takes food from shrubs and trees. Feeding is often opportunistic, and the species benefits from a mixture of vegetation, fruiting plants, and lightly managed open ground.
value.behavior: The Tropical Mockingbird is active, conspicuous, and strongly territorial. It often perches in exposed positions and sings from shrubs, fences, wires, or treetops. Birds may chase intruders and perform noticeable wing or tail movements during displays. Outside territorial interactions, they frequently forage alone or in pairs. Their tolerance of gardens, farms, and settlements allows them to remain common in many modified landscapes.

conservation.populationTrend: The species remains widespread and adaptable, although some populations may be affected by continuing habitat changes. A precise global population trend is not established here.
